title: Rigidity of the Turing degrees
formal:
Let \(D_T=\mathcal P(\mathbb N)/{\equiv_T}\) be the set of all Turing degrees, ordered by Turing reducibility. Is this order rigid? The exact assertion is
\[\forall\pi:D_T\to D_T,\quad \Bigl[\pi\text{ is bijective}\ \land\ \forall a,b\in D_T\,\bigl(a\le_T b\iff\pi(a)\le_T\pi(b)\bigr)\Bigr]\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall a\in D_T\,\pi(a)=a.\]
The domain is the full quotient of all subsets of the standard natural numbers. The quantifier over \(\pi\) ranges over arbitrary functions on this quotient in ordinary classical set theory, with ZFC as the set-theoretic background.
definitions:
Write \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), \(\mathcal P(\mathbb N)\) for its full power set, and \(\chi_A:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}\) for a set's characteristic function. A deterministic oracle Turing machine is a finite program with ordinary unbounded work tapes and an additional operation that receives \(\chi_B(k)\) when it asks whether \(k\) belongs to the oracle set \(B\). Each terminating computation takes finitely many steps and makes finitely many queries; no uniform bound on their number, time or space is imposed. Natural inputs and queries have the usual finite binary encodings. Any fixed effective enumeration \((\Phi_e)_{e\in\mathbb N}\) of all such programs gives
\[A\le_T B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists e\in\mathbb N\ \forall n\in\mathbb N,\ \Phi_e^B(n)\text{ halts with output }\chi_A(n).\]
The same index must work on every input, but may depend on \(A,B\). Programs contain no additional oracle, infinite advice or noncomputable constants. All subsets are eligible oracle sets, including noncomputable ones.

Define \(A\equiv_T B\) by \(A\le_T B\) and \(B\le_T A\). A degree \([A]\) is the equivalence class of \(A\), and \([A]\le_T[B]\) means \(A\le_T B\); this is independent of the representatives. Equality of degrees is mutual reducibility, not equality of their representatives. The set \(D_T\) includes every degree, not just degrees containing computably enumerable sets, arithmetical degrees, or degrees below a selected bound. A set is computably enumerable if a program with no oracle lists exactly its members, with arbitrary repetition and delay allowed.

An order automorphism is a total injective and surjective map \(\pi:D_T\to D_T\) that preserves and reflects every reducibility comparison. It need not be computable, definable, continuous or induced by a prescribed operation on sets. A representation \(F:\mathcal P(\mathbb N)\to\mathcal P(\mathbb N)\), if used to specify it, must satisfy \([F(A)]=\pi([A])\) for every \(A\); the representation itself need not be bijective. The order language has only equality and \(\le_T\). Jump preservation is a known consequence of this order structure, not an extra assumption in the target.

For the dated context, \(\mathbf 0=[\varnothing]\). The join \([A]\vee[B]\) is \([A\oplus B]\), where \(A\oplus B=\{2n:n\in A\}\cup\{2n+1:n\in B\}\). Set \(A'=\{e:\Phi_e^A(e)\text{ halts}\}\); the Turing jump is \([A]'=[A']\), and \(\mathbf 0''=(\mathbf 0')'\). These degrees are independent of the chosen effective machine enumeration. The upper cone with base \(b\) is \(\{a:b\le_T a\}\). Its complement includes both degrees below \(b\) and degrees incomparable with \(b\).

The assertion concerns the degree order built from the full power set in the ambient universe, not a selected countable model's internally computed degrees. The continuum hypothesis and determinacy are not hypotheses of the target. There are no finite input sizes, efficiency bounds or numerical approximation parameters in this structural question.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed universal assertion or its exact negation. A positive answer must apply to every set-theoretic order automorphism of the entire \(D_T\). A negative answer must prove
\[\exists\pi:D_T\to D_T\ \exists a\in D_T,\quad\pi\text{ is bijective},\quad \forall b,c\in D_T\,\bigl(b\le_Tc\iff\pi(b)\le_T\pi(c)\bigr),\quad\pi(a)\ne a.\]
An existence proof is sufficient; no computable formula for the automorphism is required. A construction on representatives must establish that it descends to this full quotient and has all the stated properties. Proving rigidity only on a proper substructure or for a restricted family of maps does not meet the criterion. Nor does a non-surjective order embedding or a permutation of representatives that fixes every degree. Both answer directions retain the stated classical background without an unproved extra hypothesis; relative consistency or independence alone does not assert either of these two mathematical conclusions. All supporting formalized definitions and theorems needed for the chosen direction must be included or supplied by verified Lean libraries.
why: Rigidity asks whether the entire ordering of relative computational power has any nontrivial global symmetry. Its connection with intrinsic definability and second-order arithmetic makes it a central structural question in computability, beyond the classification of individual computable problems.

importance.reason: A defining open problem of degree theory, closely tied to the intrinsic definability of computational structure and constrained by deep but incomplete rigidity theorems.

progress.text: Nerode and Shore proved that each automorphism is the identity on some upper cone. Kjos-Hanssen’s introduction distinguishes this from the later common \(\mathbf 0''\) cone bound.
Shore and Slaman proved order-theoretic definability of the Turing jump; the inspected author manuscript states the conclusion as Theorem 1.15.
Cooper announced a nontrivial automorphism of the full degree order. The later survey reports its construction as not independently verified; this review does not certify the claim.

Slaman’s published survey states rigidity on the cone above \(\mathbf 0''\), countability of the automorphism group and equivalence between full rigidity and its bi-interpretability conjecture. It retains the global question as open.
Slaman and Soskova’s journal article gives finite automorphism bases and related definability results for \(D_T(\le_T\mathbf 0')\), without proving local or global rigidity.

Kjos-Hanssen’s preprint and later journal publication exclude nontrivial automorphisms induced by coordinate permutations or by homeomorphisms preserving all Bernoulli measures. The preprint record remains version 1.

Ongay-Valverde’s version 1 gives a conditional restriction on genericity of degrees and their images; Theorem 7.4 and its Section 8 consequences assume the continuum hypothesis. The complete proof was not independently certified in this review.

context_blocks.text: Two oracle decision problems represent the same Turing degree precisely when each can compute the other. Their degree records computational power without committing to a particular set of integers as its encoding. This question asks whether all degrees can be consistently relabeled, changing at least one point while preserving every reducibility comparison. A nontrivial symmetry must work simultaneously across the whole structure.

The computable degree \(\mathbf 0\) and the join operation are fixed by every order automorphism. Shore and Slaman proved the stronger fact that the graph of the Turing jump is first-order definable using the degree order alone. Thus \(\pi(a')=\pi(a)'\) for every degree \(a\), and all finite jumps of \(\mathbf 0\) are fixed. Preservation of the jump is an established restriction, not a proof of full rigidity.

Slaman and Woodin proved that every automorphism fixes every degree at least \(\mathbf 0''\); their automorphism group is also at most countable. These are statements about restrictions of global automorphisms. They do not assert that an arbitrary automorphism of the upper cone extends to the full structure, and they do not cover degrees incomparable with its base. The underlying set of all degrees has cardinality \(2^{\aleph_0}\).

The same structural analysis connects rigidity with the Slaman–Woodin bi-interpretability conjecture: the degree structure and full second-order arithmetic would recover one another through logical interpretations, with the correspondence to degrees definable without parameters. The survey states equivalence with rigidity in its precise sense of bi-interpretability. This concerns the expressive power of the whole order.

Rigidity does not mean that every degree has its own parameter-free first-order definition. There are only countably many finite formulas in this language and uncountably many degrees. Most degrees therefore cannot be individually defined that way, even if the entire order is rigid.

Kjos-Hanssen proves that a coordinate permutation \(p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), acting on characteristic sequences by \(F_p(A)(n)=A(p(n))\), can induce an automorphism of all Turing degrees only when that automorphism is the identity; in fact \(p\) must be computable. He also excludes nontrivial automorphisms induced by homeomorphisms of \(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) preserving every Bernoulli product measure. Here the topology is generated by finite initial segments, and the measure with parameter \(t\in[0,1]\) makes coordinates independent bits with probability \(t\) of being one. These representation and measure restrictions are absent from the main question.

Slaman and Soskova study the separate structure of degrees at most \(\mathbf 0'\), equivalently the \(\Delta^0_2\) degrees. They prove that this local structure has a finite automorphism base: agreement on a fixed finite tuple determines an automorphism. They obtain a countable automorphism group and an equivalence between local rigidity and bi-interpretability with first-order arithmetic. None of these conclusions states that the group is trivial. Their local arithmetic comparison is distinct from the full structure’s second-order comparison.

Ongay-Valverde’s 2021 preprint gives restrictions on the action of a hypothetical automorphism on generic degrees under the continuum hypothesis \(2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_1\). Theorem 7.4 additionally concerns families meeting a relative genericity condition above every degree, with jointly generic representatives for each degree and its image. Its Section 8 explicitly keeps the continuum-hypothesis assumption. This conditional restriction neither constructs a nontrivial automorphism nor proves that all automorphisms are trivial, even under that hypothesis.

Cooper’s 1999 Theorem 1.1 claims a nonidentity global automorphism fixing every degree at least \(\mathbf 0'\). This is a claim of a full negative answer, rather than merely a local example. The present review checked the statement in the author-uploaded text but did not verify its long construction.

Slaman’s later survey explicitly reports that Cooper’s construction had not been independently verified and treats the general problem as unresolved. The subsequent permutation paper also states the full question as open. The card therefore keeps the historical full-solution claim visible and uses uncertain status; it does not infer either correctness or a proved error from the announcement alone.

sentences: Turing degrees identify oracle sets that compute one another, and their order compares relative computational power.
The question asks whether every bijection of all degrees that preserves and reflects this order fixes every degree.
The target allows arbitrary set-theoretic automorphisms and requires a complete Lean proof of rigidity or of a nontrivial global automorphism.
Known jump, cone, representation and local-structure results impose substantial restrictions without settling the entire order.
Cooper’s historical full-solution claim remains explicitly separated from verified partial results, and the card records uncertain status because its construction was reported as unverified.
